intro: Naomi Prescott has been promoted to Head of Information Security at Halden Mutual, a mid-sized insurer. She was a strong technician, but the board is now asking her questions about risk, law, money and people, and none of them are about firewalls. She decides to prepare for the CISSP and to learn how to think like a leader.
Follow Naomi through her first year, from the board room to the server room and back.

security-governance-ethics-legal: After a minor breach, the board asks why a weakness in the claims portal was written down a year ago and never fixed. Naomi learns that security starts at the top: who directs it, who is accountable, and what reasonable care looks like. She also meets the ethics she will be held to and the privacy laws that shape what she may do with customer data.
risk-management-threat-modeling: Naomi is asked whether a $30,000-a-year web application firewall is worth it. She learns to put numbers on risk: what an attack is expected to cost each year before and after the control. She also learns how risk can be treated, how threats are modelled before systems are built, and how a vendor’s weaknesses become Halden’s own.
continuity-personnel-security: The online claims platform must come back in twelve hours with at most five minutes of lost transactions. Naomi works out which kind of recovery site and replication can meet that, and how the plan is tested without disrupting business. She also looks at people: how to stop one person controlling a whole process, and what to do when staff join and leave.
asset-classification-data-lifecycle: Halden is replacing a rack of drives that held customer records, and someone suggests selling them. Naomi learns that data needs an owner, a classification and a plan for the end of its life, and that ‘deleted’ is not the same as ‘gone’. A research group asks for data too, which teaches her about masking and protecting identity.
security-models-design-principles: The firm builds a system for analysts who serve two competing banks. Naomi learns how formal security models prevent an analyst who has seen one bank’s files from seeing the other’s. She also learns the design principles that sit under all security decisions: least privilege, fail securely, defence in depth, and not trusting anything by default.
system-architectures-vulnerabilities: Halden moves claims processing to small serverless functions and puts analytics boxes in its depots. One function turns out to have administrator rights to the whole account. Naomi learns the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture type, the hardware and software protections that sit beneath them, and why every system has a life cycle.
site-facility-environment: The data room is moving to a basement next to a loading dock, with one water sprinkler, a single standby power unit and no environmental sensors. Naomi learns how sites are chosen and protected in layers, how fire, power and climate are controlled, and why the wiring closet matters as much as the server.
cryptography-pki: A partner needs signed, confidential files. A recent breach also showed that unsalted password hashes were cracked in hours. Naomi learns the differences between symmetric and asymmetric encryption, hashing and signing, how certificates and authorities create trust, and how keys are looked after in practice.
network-architecture-segmentation: After an attacker took over a web server and scanned the internal network, Naomi redesigns it in zones. She learns how network models describe what each device does, how segmentation and a screened subnet contain damage, and which perimeter defences look at which layer.
secure-communications-wireless: Staff use full-tunnel VPN, administrators use an unencrypted remote login, and the Wi-Fi passphrase is known to someone who has left. Naomi replaces each weak link: encrypted protocols, central authentication, individual wireless logins, and protections for email against spoofing.
network-transport-edge-operations: Voice calls stutter at peak hours across forty branches. Naomi learns how traffic is carried, what separates the planes of a network device, how performance is measured, and what is different in cloud networks. She also reviews a vendor who has a permanent remote account into Halden’s network.
iam-authentication-access-models: Administrators should manage routers with per-command control and a full record, while branch staff reach core applications only from compliant devices in working hours. Naomi learns how people are identified and verified, how biometrics are measured, and the models that decide who can do what.
iam-federation-lifecycle-pam: After an acquisition, there are sixty cloud apps, three directories, constant password resets, former contractors still active and a shared admin login. Naomi learns how federation and single sign-on reduce the pain, how access follows people as they join, move and leave, and how the most powerful accounts are controlled.
assessment-testing-audit: Customers want proof that Halden’s controls work, and Naomi also wants to know whether an attacker could reach customer data. Those are two different questions. She learns when to commission an audit, a scan or a penetration test, how tests are scoped, and how to turn the results into decisions.
ops-monitoring-incident-forensics: A workstation is calling a known malicious address at night. Naomi’s team confirms it, isolates it and preserves evidence in the right order, so it would stand up in court if needed. She learns how logging and monitoring catch problems, and how an incident moves from detection to lessons learned.
ops-resilience-change-physical: A hospital client’s billing system has strict recovery targets. Naomi helps design the backups, replication and alternate site to meet them, tests the plan, and learns how patching and changes are controlled so that fixing one thing does not break another. Physical safety of staff turns out to be part of operations too.
sdlc-secure-development: Halden’s developers ship every two weeks. Naomi works with them to put threat modelling into design, security checks into the pipeline, and a bill of materials into every release. She learns the common coding flaws, the tests that find them, and how to decide whether to trust software someone else wrote.
software-ecosystem-acquired-software: A review of the new mobile app finds unlimited API query depth, a leaked key and a dependency pulled from the wrong registry. Naomi learns how the whole ecosystem fits together, from languages and libraries to build servers and repositories, and how to assess commercial, open-source and managed software before relying on it.

epilogue: On the morning of the exam Naomi is calmer than she expected. She has been answering these questions all year in meetings, from the board down to the server room. The exam asks for the judgement of a manager, not a technician, and she has been practising exactly that.

security-governance-ethics-legal: After the breach, Naomi’s first instinct is to buy a new firewall. The board is not asking about firewalls; it is asking who was responsible for fixing a known weakness and why nobody did. Governance questions rarely have technical answers. The firewall arrives in a very handsome box and answers nothing.
risk-management-threat-modeling: A manager buys cyber insurance and declares the risk ‘gone’. Naomi points out that insurance transfers part of the cost, not the responsibility, and that some risk always remains. Only management can formally accept what is left. The manager looks at the policy and the policy, being a document, says nothing.
continuity-personnel-security: Naomi’s recovery plan promises the claims platform back in twelve hours. Nobody asked the business owners what an hour of downtime costs. The numbers, when finally supplied, make the twelve-hour plan look like a leisurely stroll. The impact analysis should have come first, and it should have come from the people who feel the pain.
asset-classification-data-lifecycle: A custodian quietly decides which data is confidential, because ‘someone has to’. The owner, finding out, is displeased. Classification is the owner’s job; the custodian protects what the owner decides. Meanwhile, the old drives were degaussed, which works on magnetic media and does precisely nothing for solid-state ones.
security-models-design-principles: A designer applies the model that protects confidentiality to a system whose real goal is integrity, and the whole design points the wrong way. Bell-LaPadula and Biba are mirror images. The designer is gently asked what the system is for, which is the question that should come before the diagram.
system-architectures-vulnerabilities: The team enables address randomisation and memory protections on the old server and declares the bug ‘fixed’. The bug remains; it is just harder to exploit. A harder door to open is not a wall. The function with administrator rights to everything, meanwhile, waits patiently in the cloud, like a spare key under the mat.
site-facility-environment: The facilities manager installs a carbon dioxide fire system in the occupied server room, with no alarm and no delay. It is brilliant at putting out fires and rather less brilliant at keeping the technicians alive. Naomi suggests a clean agent, an alarm and a delay, in that order, and a conversation with the safety officer.
cryptography-pki: A developer uses a hash to ‘authenticate’ messages. Anyone who can change the message can recompute the hash. A hash shows that something is unchanged, not who made it. A keyed signature does that. The developer’s messages, until then, were as authentic as a handwritten note saying ‘trust me’.
network-architecture-segmentation: An engineer separates the servers into VLANs and declares the network ‘segmented’ and ‘secure’. A VLAN is a way to separate traffic, not a security boundary, and the routing between VLANs let everything through. The attacker, who had only been interested in a small tour, took the long one.
secure-communications-wireless: The firm rolls out ‘encrypted’ open Wi-Fi and tells staff they are safe. The traffic is encrypted, but the access point is not authenticated, so staff can connect to a clever fake with the same name. Encryption without knowing who you are talking to is a secret whispered to a stranger.
network-transport-edge-operations: Someone says the carrier’s private circuit is ‘secure because it is private’. Private is not encrypted. The carrier’s staff, and anyone who taps the line, can see the traffic. The branch manager, who thought ‘private’ meant ‘sealed’, goes pale at the word ‘plaintext’.
iam-authentication-access-models: The bank introduces ‘multi-factor’ sign-in using a password and a memorable answer. The auditor, a calm person with an unhurried pen, notes that both are knowledge factors. One kind of factor, twice, is still one kind. The auditor writes ‘finding’ and underlines it twice, which is, one supposes, two underlines of the same kind.
iam-federation-lifecycle-pam: After single sign-on goes live, someone relaxes the MFA requirement because ‘there’s only one login now’. Single sign-on makes one login very valuable and very tempting. Strong MFA matters more, not less. Meanwhile, a contractor’s account from 2019 is still happily active.
assessment-testing-audit: A manager commissions a vulnerability scan and tells the board that Halden has been ‘penetration tested’. A scan finds weaknesses; a penetration test tries to use them, with written permission. The two are different jobs with different reports. The board, to its credit, asks a good follow-up question, which is not what the manager hoped for.
ops-monitoring-incident-forensics: A responder rebuilds the compromised workstation immediately, in the interest of a quick recovery. The memory, the logs and the evidence go with it. Contain first, preserve, then rebuild. The workstation is delightfully clean and utterly mute.
ops-resilience-change-physical: The team installs mirrored disks and tells the board that ransomware is no longer a concern. Ransomware encrypts both disks happily; mirroring faithfully copies the damage. RAID protects against a failed disk, not a bad day. Naomi holds up a photocopier and says that it is also very good at duplicating mistakes.
sdlc-secure-development: The security review is scheduled for the week before launch. It finds forty issues, three of them serious. The launch is delayed, the developers are cross, and everyone agrees that this was foreseeable. Security checks belong early, when changes are cheap, and not at the end, when everything is expensive and awkward.
software-ecosystem-acquired-software: A developer hides the admin button in the mobile app and calls it ‘access control’. Anyone who can call the API directly can still reach the function. Client-side hiding is a curtain, not a door. The reviewer opens the curtain, finds the function behind it and wonders where to put the lock.

security-governance-ethics-legal.problem: Security decisions are technical when they should be accountable and lawful.
security-governance-ethics-legal.cause: Governance, ethics and legal duties are treated as someone else’s concern.
security-governance-ethics-legal.solution: Governance structures, due care and diligence, the code of ethics and privacy law give direction and accountability.

risk-management-threat-modeling.problem: Money is spent on controls without knowing what they are worth.
risk-management-threat-modeling.cause: Risk is not measured and responsibility is confused with cost transfer.
risk-management-threat-modeling.solution: Quantitative and qualitative risk analysis, treatment options, threat modelling and supply chain review support choices.

continuity-personnel-security.problem: Disruption stops the business and people are part of the risk.
continuity-personnel-security.cause: Recovery targets and impact are guessed.
continuity-personnel-security.solution: The business impact analysis, recovery objectives, sites, testing and personnel controls give a plan.

asset-classification-data-lifecycle.problem: Data is not classified or protected through its life.
asset-classification-data-lifecycle.cause: Owners and custodians are confused and disposal is careless.
asset-classification-data-lifecycle.solution: Classification, ownership, lifecycle controls, privacy techniques and correct sanitisation protect data to the end.
asset-classification-data-lifecycle.next: Next, the models and principles behind secure design.

security-models-design-principles.problem: Systems are designed without a clear security rationale.
security-models-design-principles.cause: Models and principles are mixed up.
security-models-design-principles.solution: Formal models, design principles, trust in hardware and physical security give a foundation.

system-architectures-vulnerabilities.problem: Each architecture has its own weak spots.
system-architectures-vulnerabilities.cause: Protections are assumed to remove bugs and ownership is unclear.
system-architectures-vulnerabilities.solution: Hardware and software capabilities and the typical weaknesses of each architecture type show where to look.

site-facility-environment.problem: Physical sites are exposed to intruders and environmental hazards.
site-facility-environment.cause: Location, fire, power and cooling are afterthoughts.
site-facility-environment.solution: Layered site design, environmental controls, fire suppression and power protection secure the site.

cryptography-pki.problem: Data must be protected and its origin proven.
cryptography-pki.cause: Algorithms and keys are mixed up and badly managed.
cryptography-pki.solution: Encryption, hashing, signatures, certificates and key management protect and prove.

network-architecture-segmentation.cause: Networks are flat and rely on the perimeter.
network-architecture-segmentation.solution: Layered models, segmentation, screened subnets and perimeter defences contain attackers.

secure-communications-wireless.cause: Weak protocols and shared secrets persist.
secure-communications-wireless.solution: TLS, IPsec, VPNs, central authentication and modern wireless protect communications.

network-transport-edge-operations.problem: Networks perform poorly and carry hidden risk.
network-transport-edge-operations.cause: Transport, edge and third-party links are assumed safe.
network-transport-edge-operations.solution: Plane separation, performance measures, SDN, cloud networks and monitoring cover them.

iam-authentication-access-models.cause: Factors are miscounted and models misapplied.
iam-authentication-access-models.solution: Factors, biometrics, Kerberos and access control models give strong authentication and authorisation.

iam-federation-lifecycle-pam.problem: Identity sprawl, orphaned accounts and powerful access.
iam-federation-lifecycle-pam.cause: Many directories and no lifecycle control.
iam-federation-lifecycle-pam.solution: Federation, SSO, joiner-mover-leaver, reviews and privileged access management bring control.

assessment-testing-audit.problem: Nobody knows whether the controls work.
assessment-testing-audit.cause: Testing is confused with auditing and scores with risk.
assessment-testing-audit.solution: Assessments, audits, scans, penetration tests and metrics provide evidence.
assessment-testing-audit.next: Next, operations: monitoring, incidents and forensics.

ops-monitoring-incident-forensics.problem: Attacks go undetected and evidence is destroyed.
ops-monitoring-incident-forensics.solution: Logging, SIEM, the incident lifecycle and forensic handling detect and preserve.
ops-monitoring-incident-forensics.next: Next, resilience, change and physical operations.

ops-resilience-change-physical.cause: Recovery targets are loose and changes are uncontrolled.
ops-resilience-change-physical.solution: Objectives, backups, alternate sites, testing and change management keep operations resilient.

sdlc-secure-development.problem: Flaws are found late and are expensive.
sdlc-secure-development.cause: Security is added at the end.
sdlc-secure-development.solution: Shifting security left, secure coding and testing, and sensible controls reduce flaws.

software-ecosystem-acquired-software.problem: Third-party code and tooling add risk.
software-ecosystem-acquired-software.cause: Components and services are trusted without checking.
software-ecosystem-acquired-software.solution: API, build and supply chain security, and assessment of acquired software manage the risk.
software-ecosystem-acquired-software.next: That completes the lessons. Next come the cheat sheet, the word bank and the practice questions.
